results.question: We're a state agriculture department planning a phone-based voice advisory for small farmers in Odia. What should we watch out for?

old.answer:
A few things from documented deployments are worth flagging for a phone-based agricultural advisory in a regional language:

- **Data ownership at the department level** — MahaVISTAAR, a voice advisory Maharashtra's government runs for farmers, found that mandi price data with a 48-hour lag caused wrong harvest-timing advice. The fix wasn't technical — it was a governance call with the data owner to shift update cadence to 6 hours. - **Audio data collection for the voice layer** — the Bhili Language Enablement pathway (a government effort to build a voice AI for tribal farmers in Nandurbar) found that collecting clean, studio-quality audio from young, standard-dialect speakers produced a model that failed on actual phone calls. - **Governance before launch** — MahaVISTAAR's pathway documents six questions that must have named answers before any public deployment: who owns the system, who approves what it can say, who decides what it must not say, who reviews failures, who updates the knowledge base, and who handles complaints. If any answer is "we'll figure it out," the deployment isn't ready.
- **Safety test bank** — documented across multiple voice AI deployments: build a set of test cases covering out-of-scope questions, distress scenarios, and inappropriate prompts before launch, not after. results.question: Compare how MahaVISTAAR and the African Voice AI project in Kenya handled local languages.
results.expect: Both pathways compared (explicitly requested), each described in a few words, neutral, concise.

old.answer:
Both are voice AI deployments for smallholder farmers, but they faced different language problems and solved them differently.

- **MahaVISTAAR's challenge was dialect variation at scale** — Marathi is the primary language, but regional dialects and vocabulary (crop names, pest names, scheme names, mandi terms) caused ASR and retrieval failures. The fix was a bilingual Marathi↔English agricultural glossary, now available as a reusable asset via OpenAgriNet.
- **The African Voice AI's challenge was code-switching within a single sentence** — Kenyan farmers and field agents routinely mix Kiswahili and English mid-utterance. The base Msingi AI models supported only pure Kiswahili, so code-switching had to be engineered into the ASR and TTS layers separately — the LLM handled it natively, but that didn't propagate to the speech layers automatically.
- **A concrete downstream consequence in Kenya:** a text normaliser (which assumes one output language) broke mid-sentence in code-switched replies, so number-spelling was delegated to the language model itself, in whichever language it was using in that sentence.
- **One thing both show:** language work doesn't end with the model — it surfaces in data (glossaries, agricultural vocabulary), in the speech pipeline (ASR/TTS accuracy), and in the conversational design (pacing, vocabulary assumed of the speaker). MahaVISTAAR absorbed this over nine months of build; the African deployment hit it during the Define stage adaptation phase.

The African Voice AI pathway (documented August 2026) is still pre-pilot, so there's no field data yet on how the code-switching fix holds against real telephony audio with real users.

judge.notes: Compares both requested pathways in a neutral tone, with brief context (voice AI for smallholder farmers, Marathi vs. Kiswahili/English). But it uses a lot of unexplained jargon (ASR, TTS, LLM, text normaliser, mandi, Msingi AI, OpenAgriNet, 'Define stage adaptation phase'), and the text-normaliser bullet adds detail most users won't need.

new.answer:
Both pathways dealt with language as a technical and institutional challenge, but at very different layers of the stack.

- **What the language gap actually was** — MahaVISTAAR's challenge was reaching farmers who spoke Marathi and had no text literacy, so the question was channel (voice was the only viable interface) and institutional trust (the voice had to carry government authority to be acted on). The African Voice AI team's challenge was more structural: their ASR and TTS models were trained on Kiswahili alone, but Kenyan callers routinely switch between Kiswahili and English mid-sentence, so the speech layers broke even when the underlying language model handled it fine.
- **The fix in each case** — MahaVISTAAR's language work was largely a design and federation decision: Marathi as the primary voice, with proactive outreach built to find farmers rather than wait for them to call. African Voice AI had to engineer code-switching into the speech models themselves — and separately, stop using a text normaliser for numbers, because a normaliser has to assume one output language and fails mid-sentence in a mixed reply.
- **What didn't transfer automatically** — African Voice AI reused an India-built orchestration stack (the same ecosystem MahaVISTAAR drew on), and the team was explicit that porting the stack saved substantial integration time but that local language adaptation — code-switching, response-style tuning, provider-specific channel work — had to be budgeted and executed as a separate phase. The build compressed, but the language work didn't come along for free.
- **One gap worth noting** — as of August 2026, the African Voice AI team had not yet benchmarked their code-switching fix against real, accented, noisy telephony audio; all their latency and accuracy figures were measured on clean test audio. MahaVISTAAR's production data at scale (342K+ users, 1.67M+ questions) gives it a much deeper evidence base on what actually holds in the field.

results.question: How did teams get rural users to actually trust and use a voice assistant?
results.expect: Answers from the single best-fitting pathway (described in a few words), short, neutral, plain words; ends with a short question about that same pathway, not a second pathway.

old.answer:
The honest answer is: they didn't trust the *voice assistant*. They trusted the institution behind it. That's the finding that shows up across multiple pathways — MahaVISTAAR and Voice AI for Inclusion both make this explicit.

In Maharashtra, women farmers were getting contradictory advice from fertiliser sellers who had a commercial incentive to sell. When the same question got answered by a government-backed voice in Marathi — a language they actually understood — the trust equation changed. Not because the AI was impressive, but because the answer came from a source they already had reason to trust.

The flip side is worth knowing too: if the institution itself isn't trusted, voice AI amplifies that deficit rather than fixing it. It's not a trust-building tool on its own.

The other thing that mattered was **channel fit**. MahaVISTAAR's target users were feature-phone-dependent, Marathi-speaking, and text-illiterate — voice wasn't a preference, it was the only interface that could work. Bhili Language Enablement adds another layer: for tribal women in Nandurbar who had far less Marathi exposure than men who left for work, hearing the advisory in their own language (Dehwali Bhili) was itself a trust signal.

And Amul's Sarla Ben found something interesting about *when* trust shows up in usage data: peaks at **6–9am and 6–9pm** — exactly the milking windows. The design matched the actual use moment, which is its own form of trust-building.

results.question: What did they get wrong early on, and what did they change?
results.expect: Neutral description of early setbacks and changes (no "flopped"/"failed miserably"), short, plain words, ends with a question about this same pathway.

old.answer:
Three things went wrong early, and each one led to a concrete fix.

The first was **consent**. The district team in Dharwad wanted to convert existing government data directly into Blue Dots — the data already existed, so why not use it? The team pushed back hard: holding data and holding consent to use it in a new way are two completely different things. They built a direct communication process to reach each person individually, explain the initiative, and get proper consent before creating any record.

The second was **data freshness**. Even after consent was sorted, government-held data turned out to be stale — people's situations had already changed since the data was collected. The fix wasn't a one-time cleanup; it became an ongoing operational discipline. This is still not fully resolved — at the time the pathway was documented (September 2026), they were still working on how to treat the data as a shared public rail rather than a single-purpose dataset.

The third was **dialect**. The speech model was initially tuned on standard Kannada as spoken in Bangalore. Dharwad Kannada is faster and uses vocabulary that simply doesn't appear in that training data. Engagement measurably dropped. The fix was building a local glossary and adjusting the conversational tone and pacing to match how people actually talk there. The lesson they drew: dialect adaptation is local and non-optional — you can't inherit it from a neighboring deployment even if it's technically the "same" language.

The bigger pattern across all three is that the failures were predictable in retrospect, and each one is now a named precondition for the next adopter rather than a surprise to stumble into.
